summary: Gives details for using the DES encryption standard to encrypt PPP packets. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 2419.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret code machine that scrambles the data on a link so eavesdroppers cannot read it.

questions: how to encrypt ppp with des
how does cipher block chaining work
what is a nonce in cryptography
subtitle: Encrypting point-to-point links using the DES algorithm

tldr.problem: Network links need privacy protection, but there was no standard way to encrypt PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) traffic using DES, a widely available encryption algorithm.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1969 specifies how to apply DES encryption in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode to PPP packets, with a 56-bit key and a sequence number to handle packet loss and chaining across multiple packets.
tldr.outcome: PPP implementations can now negotiate DES encryption for privacy. The RFC was replaced by RFC 2419, which provides a newer approach to PPP encryption.

today: RFC 1969 is Informational and was superseded by RFC 2419 in June 1996. RFC 2419 provides a different approach to PPP encryption using triple DES and other improvements. DES itself has been deprecated in favor of stronger algorithms like AES due to its 56-bit key size being considered too short by modern standards.

sections.title: Why Encrypt PPP Links
sections.content: PPP is the protocol used for point-to-point links, such as dial-up modem connections or leased lines. Traffic on these links is often sensitive and needs to be protected from eavesdropping. DES (Data Encryption Standard) is a well-understood and widely available encryption algorithm, making it a practical choice for standardizing PPP encryption. RFC 1969 specifies how to use DES with PPP so that vendors can implement interoperable encryption. The encryption operates within the PPP Encryption Control Protocol (ECP), which negotiates parameters and algorithm choice during the connection setup.
sections.plainLanguage: When two machines talk over a phone line, anyone with the right equipment can listen in. This RFC says how to scramble the conversation so eavesdroppers cannot understand it.

sections.title: How the Encryption Works
sections.content: DES encryption requires a shared secret key (56 bits long) that both sender and receiver must know. During the ECP negotiation phase, each side offers a configuration option containing an 8-byte nonce (a random value used only once). This nonce serves as the initialization vector for the encryption. Once encryption is negotiated and activated, the sender encrypts the PPP packet's protocol and data fields using DES in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode. Each packet is prefixed with a 16-bit sequence number so the receiver can detect lost packets and maintain correct chaining across packet boundaries. The receiver decrypts the ciphertext using the same key and nonce, recovering the original packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Two machines agree on a secret code and a starting value. Then every packet gets scrambled with that code using a chain method where each packet depends on the previous one, with a number on each packet so if one is lost you can still decode the rest.

sections.title: Configuration and Packet Format
sections.content: The DESE (DES Encryption) configuration option is sent during ECP negotiation. It contains a type field (value 1 for DESE), a length field (always 10), and an 8-byte initial nonce. The nonce should be a unique value for each negotiation, for example based on the current time and nanoseconds. Once ECP reaches the Opened state and encryption begins, packets are sent with a protocol ID of 0x53 (or 0x55 for multilink), a 16-bit sequence number starting from 0, and the encrypted payload. The sequence number allows recovery if some packets are lost in transit: if packet N is lost but N+1 and N+2 arrive, the decoder can still decrypt N+1 and later packets because it only needs the ciphertext of the previous packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Before encrypting, the machines exchange a starting secret number. Then each encrypted packet has its own number, starting from 0 and counting up, so if a packet gets lost the machines can keep working.

sections.title: Padding and Encryption Process
sections.content: DES operates on 64-bit (8-byte) blocks, so packets that are not a multiple of 8 bytes must be padded. For protocols with explicit length fields (like IP), random bytes can be added as padding; the receiver ignores padding since it reads only the declared packet length. For protocols without length fields (like bridged frames), self-describing padding is needed to unambiguously remove the padding bytes. The encryption process chains blocks: the sender encodes each plaintext block using DES with the ciphertext from the previous block XORed into it. For the first packet in the connection, the previous ciphertext is the DES encryption of the initial nonce. For subsequent packets, it is the last ciphertext block of the previous packet. This chaining prevents identical plaintext blocks from producing identical ciphertext, making the encryption stronger.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets must be rounded up to 8-byte chunks by adding garbage bytes. Then each 8-byte chunk is scrambled using both the secret code and what the previous chunk turned into, so the same plaintext never looks the same twice.

sections.title: Handling Lost Packets
sections.content: Because chaining crosses packet boundaries, packet loss can be disruptive. When the receiver detects a gap in sequence numbers, it knows one or more packets were lost. If packet N-1 is lost, packet N cannot be decoded because the decoder needs the ciphertext of packet N-1 as the initialization for packet N. However, packet N+1 and all subsequent packets can still be decoded correctly because they only require the ciphertext of their previous packet, which was received. The sender includes a sequence number precisely to enable this recovery: by checking the sequence numbers, the receiver knows exactly which packets arrived and which were lost, allowing it to resynchronize at the next received packet. This graceful recovery avoids losing all subsequent packets when a single packet is dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: If a packet in the middle gets lost, the next packet cannot be decoded because the chain is broken. But the packet after that can be decoded because it chains from the one before it, which arrived. So losing one packet only breaks one decryption, then things work again.
